title: Dua for Anxiety and Grief
arabic: اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَعُوذُ بِكَ مِنَ الْهَمِّ وَالْحَزَنِ، وَالْعَجْزِ وَالْكَسَلِ، وَالْبُخْلِ وَالْجُبْنِ، وَضَلَعِ الدَّيْنِ وَغَلَبَةِ الرِّجَالِ
transliteration: Allahumma inni a'udhu bika minal-hammi wal-hazan, wal-'ajzi wal-kasal, wal-bukhli wal-jubn, wa dala'id-dayni wa ghalabatir-rijal.
translation: O Allah, I seek refuge in You from anxiety and grief, from helplessness and laziness, from cowardice and miserliness, from being overcome by debt and overpowered by men.
context: The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) taught this dua to his companions as a comprehensive shield against the mental and emotional burdens of daily life. Anas ibn Malik reported that the Prophet used to recite this often, showing that even the most beloved of creation sought Allah's protection from the weight of worry. It is a reminder that anxiety is not a spiritual failing — it is a human condition the Prophet himself addressed head-on, with words rather than avoidance.

title: Verily, With Hardship Comes Ease
arabic: فَإِنَّ مَعَ الْعُسْرِ يُسْرًا (٥) إِنَّ مَعَ الْعُسْرِ يُسْرًا (٦)
transliteration: Fa inna ma'al-'usri yusra. Inna ma'al-'usri yusra.
translation: So verily, with hardship comes ease. Verily, with hardship comes ease.
context: Revealed to comfort the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) during a period of intense difficulty in Makkah, this verse repeats itself twice for emphasis — classical Arabic scholars note that the definite article on 'hardship' (al-'usr) refers to the same single hardship, while 'ease' (yusr) is indefinite, appearing twice, implying that one hardship is always accompanied by multiple eases. It is one of the most recited verses for reassurance in the Quran, teaching that difficulty and relief are never separate; ease is woven into the hardship itself, not merely after it.

title: Dua for Seeking Forgiveness (Sayyid al-Istighfar)
arabic: اللَّهُمَّ أَنْتَ رَبِّي لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا أَنْتَ، خَلَقْتَنِي وَأَنَا عَبْدُكَ، وَأَنَا عَلَى عَهْدِكَ وَوَعْدِكَ مَا اسْتَطَعْتُ، أَعُوذُ بِكَ مِنْ شَرِّ مَا صَنَعْتُ، أَبُوءُ لَكَ بِنِعْمَتِكَ عَلَيَّ، وَأَبُوءُ بِذَنْبِي فَاغْفِرْ لِي فَإِنَّهُ لَا يَغْفِرُ الذُّنُوبَ إِلَّا أَنْتَ
transliteration: Allahumma anta rabbi la ilaha illa ant, khalaqtani wa ana 'abduk, wa ana 'ala 'ahdika wa wa'dika mastata't, a'udhu bika min sharri ma sana't, abu'u laka bini'matika 'alayya, wa abu'u bidhanbi faghfir li fa'innahu la yaghfirudh-dhunuba illa ant.
translation: O Allah, You are my Lord, there is no god but You. You created me and I am Your servant, and I am faithful to Your covenant and promise as best I can. I seek refuge in You from the evil of what I have done. I acknowledge Your favor upon me, and I acknowledge my sin, so forgive me, for none forgives sins except You.
context: Known as 'the master of ways to seek forgiveness,' the Prophet (peace be upon him) said that whoever recites this during the day with certainty and dies that day before evening will be among the people of Paradise, and likewise for the night. Its structure moves the heart through acknowledgment of Allah's lordship, honest admission of one's own shortcomings, and a direct plea for mercy — a complete emotional arc from guilt to hope.

title: Allah Does Not Burden a Soul Beyond Its Capacity
arabic: لَا يُكَلِّفُ اللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا
translation: Allah does not burden a soul beyond that it can bear.
context: This closing verse of Surah Al-Baqarah is among the most frequently turned to for reassurance during trials. Scholars explain that 'wus'ha' refers to a soul's true capacity — not merely what feels bearable, but what Allah, who created that soul, knows it can carry. It is often recited alongside the understanding that trials are proportionate to one's inner strength, even when that strength is not yet visible to the person enduring it.

title: Dua for Guidance in Decisions (Istikharah)
arabic: اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَسْتَخِيرُكَ بِعِلْمِكَ، وَأَسْتَقْدِرُكَ بِقُدْرَتِكَ، وَأَسْأَلُكَ مِنْ فَضْلِكَ الْعَظِيمِ، فَإِنَّكَ تَقْدِرُ وَلَا أَقْدِرُ، وَتَعْلَمُ وَلَا أَعْلَمُ، وَأَنْتَ عَلَّامُ الْغُيُوبِ
transliteration: Allahumma inni astakhiruka bi'ilmika, wa astaqdiruka biqudratika, wa as'aluka min fadlikal-'azim, fa'innaka taqdiru wa la aqdir, wa ta'lamu wa la a'lam, wa anta 'allamul-ghuyub.
translation: O Allah, I seek Your guidance by virtue of Your knowledge, and I seek ability by virtue of Your power, and I ask You of Your great bounty. You have power and I do not, You know and I do not, and You are the Knower of the unseen.
context: Jabir ibn Abdullah narrated that the Prophet (peace be upon him) used to teach this prayer to his companions for all matters, just as he taught them chapters of the Quran — showing how central seeking guidance was to daily decision-making. It is traditionally paired with two units of voluntary prayer before major decisions, and its language deliberately places the person's limited knowledge beside Allah's complete knowledge, easing the pressure of having to know the outcome in advance.

title: Remembrance of Allah Brings Rest to the Heart
arabic: الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَتَطْمَئِنُّ قُلُوبُهُم بِذِكْرِ اللَّهِ ۗ أَلَا بِذِكْرِ اللَّهِ تَطْمَئِنُّ الْقُلُوبُ
transliteration: Alladhina amanu wa tatma'innu qulubuhum bidhikrillah, ala bidhikrillahi tatma'innul-qulub.
translation: Those who believe and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah — verily, in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest.
context: This verse describes 'itminan' — a settled, steady tranquility of the heart — as the direct fruit of dhikr (remembrance of Allah). Commentators note the verse's structure: it first states the general principle, then repeats it as an affirmed certainty ('ala', meaning 'indeed' or 'truly') to remove any doubt. It is frequently recommended for moments of gratitude and peace, as a reminder that the calm one feels is itself a sign of a connected heart, worth noticing and giving thanks for.
